name: Good Morning, Axiom
creator: Sunita Ferreira-Oduya (author); Tomás Achebe-Lindqvist (illustrator)
description: A beloved children's picture book following Axiom, a six-year-old with a starter BCI implant and a geneware-modified grandfather who glows faintly blue, as she navigates her first day at a mixed-tier community school. The book normalizes augmentation for young children while centering themes of curiosity and care, with Achebe-Lindqvist's illustrations rendered in warm, saturated colors that translate beautifully to both physical print and neural-feed visual streams. It has been in continuous publication since 2194 and is now in its ninth edition.
medium: physical picture book; neural-feed illustrated stream (child-safe BCI adaptation); audio narration
cultural_impact: One of the first widely distributed children's books to depict augmentation as mundane and familial rather than spectacular or frightening, credited by child psychologists with measurably reducing implant anxiety in children aged 4-8 during the BCI adoption surge of the late 2190s.
controversy: Anti-augmentation groups, including factions of the Flatskin movement, have repeatedly protested the book's presence in public libraries, calling it 'corponation-funded normalization propaganda.' The publisher, a mid-tier independent, denies any corporate backing, though financial records have never been fully disclosed.
story_hooks: The illustrator Achebe-Lindqvist has died and left behind unpublished pages for a tenth edition that contains imagery that makes certain people very nervous — imagery that looks like accurate schematics for something that shouldn't exist in a children's book.

A the Gray Zone community has been using bootleg physical copies of the book to teach children to read, but the copies have been modified — subtly, carefully — with additional pages that teach something else entirely.
The original manuscript's neural-feed adaptation contains a subliminal calibration sequence that was never supposed to be in a child-rated product; no one knows if it was accidental.
